seo.title: Karmic tail 18 12 21 compatibility: Moon, Hanged Man, World
seo.description: Karmic tail 18 12 21 compatibility: what the Moon, the Hanged Man and the World mean for two people, and how Ibsen's Peer Gynt tells this tail scene by scene.

title: Karmic tail 18-12-21 in compatibility: night, a threshold and a whole world
short: The couple's tail 18-12-21 begins at night and ends with a whole world, and the Hanged Man stands between them. The story was written long ago: Ibsen's Peer Gynt, the tale of Peer and Solveig. The Moon (18) is the entry to the task: the couple comes together over a fairy tale, a secret and a lot of guessing. The Hanged Man (12) is the middle: two people get stuck on a threshold, one "going roundabout", the other promising to wait. The World (21) is the main task: to make two lives into one whole and finally walk into their own house, instead of searching for "the whole world" at the far end of the earth.

sections.h2: What 18-12-21 means in a couple's destiny matrix
paragraphs: A couple's tail is three points on the line of tasks in the compatibility matrix; in the reading it is the sphere called "The couple's karmic tail". Yuliana Lisovskaya, whose book the compatibility calculation follows, calls such a triple a karmic programme, which is why people search for "18 12 21 programme". The tail is read in the order M–N–D. The entry to the task (M) is what the couple wants together, its shared language; the point stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish easily turns into resistance. The middle of the task (N) is how the couple travels from that wish to the task. The main task (D) is the central test, and it is read mainly through its minus: what the two cannot manage yet and what they have to learn.
In the tail 18-12-21 the roles fall like this:

ul: **Entry to the task — 18, The Moon.** The couple wants a shared secret: to understand each other without words, to live in its own fairy tale, to see more in each other than anyone else does. The resistance is the same Moon: guessing instead of asking, and an image instead of a person.

**Middle of the task — 12, The Hanged Man.** The road runs through a pause. Decisions are put off, one carries something heavy alone, the other waits. The pause can become a change of view, or it can stretch over years.

**Main task — 21, The World.** To build a whole: a shared world in which both stay themselves and what was started gets finished. In the minus the World is a closed circle: a private universe behind a locked door, or an endless search for "real life" somewhere else.

paragraphs: The atmosphere inside these couples is always the same: the centre of the couple's matrix holds 15, The Devil, the card of attraction and attachment. No birth date ever gives a personal matrix with 15 at the centre, so this atmosphere is born only in the couple. The couple's values are The Hermit (in 69.3% of these couples) or The Moon (in 30.7%).

Why Peer Gynt? Ibsen wrote this dramatic poem in 1867 on Ischia and in Sorrento, and the book came out on 14 November. In 1876 it was staged in Christiania with Grieg's music, and "Morning Mood", "In the Hall of the Mountain King" and "Solveig's Song" are known even to people who have never opened the play. The plot goes like this. Peer, a village liar, meets quiet Solveig at a wedding, lands among the trolls and builds a hut in the forest. Solveig comes to live with him, and he leaves, supposedly for a while, and spends decades looking for himself all over the world. The cards of the tail appear in the play in their own order: night and trolls, a half-open door, the whole world and the way home.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The Moon: "Peer, you're lying!"
paragraphs: The play opens with an accusation. The first line belongs to his mother, Åse: "Peer, you're lying!" Peer has just told her how he rode a reindeer along a mountain ridge and plunged with it into the abyss. As they fell, something whitish below rushed up to meet them: "Mother, 'twas our own reflection in the glass-smooth mountain tarn, shooting up towards the surface." The buck from above met the buck from below, and both went under. Åse gasps, thanks God for saving her son — and suddenly stops: she heard this story as a girl, and it happened to Gudbrand Glesnë. "Yes, a lie, turned topsy-turvy, can be prinked and tinselled out," she says.

The first image of the play is a man falling towards his own reflection. Waite calls the light of the Moon a reflection and puts "deception" on its list of meanings. Peer shines in exactly this way: someone else's tale told as his own, with himself as the hero.

A few scenes later Solveig enters the wedding yard, and Peer sees her the way couples with this tail first see each other: "How fair! Did ever you see the like! Looked down at her shoes and her snow-white apron—! … And carried a psalm-book wrapped up in a kerchief—!" When she hears his name, Solveig pulls her hand away: the gossip about Peer has reached her before Peer himself. Lisovskaya writes that couples with the Moon stay secretive even in the plus and so "become overgrown with rumours and false images" (our translation); for Peer and Solveig this began before they had even met. She refuses to dance, and Peer threatens her: "I can turn myself into a troll! I'll come to your bedside at midnight to-night." He says it outright: "I'm a were-wolf at night" — varulv in the original. And at once, "as if in dread", he changes his tone: "Dance with me, lass!" Her answer: "You were ugly then."

One short exchange holds the whole Moon. Desire and fear arrive together. Each meets not a person but an image: he sees a saint; she first hears the gossip, then sees a monster. Neither image is entirely a lie, and neither is the truth.

For a couple's tail, the Moon at the entry means this. The two are drawn together by a secret: the feeling that they knew each other without words, their own pet names and private jokes, talks until dawn, a shared legend about themselves — "as if we had always known each other". Lisovskaya writes that in the plus of the Moon partners understand each other by intuition and keep discovering something new in each other every year. This is the couple's shared language.

But the entry to the task sits on the line of tasks, and the same Moon turns into resistance. A fairy tale does not like questions. To "What's wrong?" one answers "Nothing", and by nightfall the other has built three versions of what happened and checked none of them. The past gets told in a flattering light, like Peer's reindeer ride. People grow jealous of things they invented. The image made at the start protects the couple as long as nobody touches it, so nobody touches it for years. Wen writes of the Moon that "the tame side and the wild side are at odds" — and that is how Peer and Solveig met: in one speech he is first a werewolf, then a suitor begging for a dance.

This Moon has arithmetic. The partner whose personal tail is 12-19-7 brings The Hanged Man to the entry; the partner with 6-20-14 brings The Lovers: 12 + 6 = 18. Our reading: one partner's suspension and the other's choice add up to a night in which the fairy tale is easy to see and the road is not.

sections.h2: The atmosphere — The Devil: the hall where the bridegroom gets a tail
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's matrix is its atmosphere, what goes on between the two away from view. Every couple with the tail 18-12-21 has 15, The Devil, here, and it follows from arithmetic. The partner with the personal tail 12-19-7 always has a personal centre of 5, The Hierophant; the partner with 6-20-14 always has 10, The Wheel of Fortune. 5 + 10 = 15. A card that never sits at the centre of a personal matrix appears only when two people are added together.

In Ibsen this atmosphere is the hall of the Dovre-King, the king of the trolls — the very hall of Grieg's "In the Hall of the Mountain King". Peer is courting the king's daughter, and the conditions are homely. First the home-brewed drink: "The cow gives cakes and the bullock mead; ask not if its taste be sour or sweet; the main matter is, and you mustn't forget it, it's all of it home-brewed." Then the clothes. Then the tail: "None comes courting my child with no tail at his rear." Peer grumbles and gives in: "It's true, as the saying goes: Man's but a mote. And it's wisest to follow the fashion a bit. Tie away!"

The most important thing the king says separately, like a motto for a coat of arms: "Out yonder, under the shining vault, among men the saying goes: 'Man, be thyself!' At home here with us, 'mid the tribe of the trolls, the saying goes: 'Troll, to thyself be—enough!'" Then he adds that "Enough" is "that most potent and sundering word". In the original the two mottoes differ by exactly one word: "Mand, vær dig selv!" and "Trold, vær dig selv — nok!". A man is told to be himself; a troll is told to be enough for himself.

The last condition is the eye. "In your left eye, first, I'll scratch you a bit, till you see awry; but all that you see will seem fine and brave." Here Peer digs in his heels. The tail, he says, is no problem — "no doubt I can loose what the Chamberlain tied" — breeches can be buttoned on again, an oath can be eaten. But "to live as a hill-troll for all one's days — to feel that one never can beat a retreat… that is a thing I can never agree to."

For the atmosphere of a couple this is an exact picture of the Devil. In the plus: a strong pull, their own customs, their own mead, their own language that outsiders watch in puzzlement. Lisovskaya writes that such partners accept each other's dark sides and speak openly about their desires. In the minus: the same "enough" — "the two of us are enough", friends slowly become superfluous, closeness turns into the only glue, the wish is to own rather than to be beside. For the sake of peace it is easy to accept small tails: the other's habits, the other's holidays, the other's catchphrases. The danger is something else — the scratched eye, when, to keep things calm, both agree to see what is crooked as beautiful. Wen writes that "The Devil is not a literal beast or demon; The Devil personifies human selfishness and indulging in that selfishness." Lisovskaya's chapter on the Devil ends with the line "no one belongs to anyone".

In the fifth act the old Dovre-King appears again and announces that Peer has lived his whole life by that motto: "You've lived as a troll, but have still kept it secret." As proof he pulls out a troll newspaper, which declares that "horns and a tail are of little importance, so long as one has but a strip of the hide". A couple's karmic tail is not about a tail either. It is about the word "enough".

sections.h2: The Boyg: an enemy that does not fight
paragraphs: From the troll hall Peer stumbles into pitch darkness. Something slimy and shapeless blocks his way. "Who are you?" — "Myself. Can you say the same?" The creature calls itself the Boyg. In the Norwegian it is Bøygen, a monster from the folk tale of Peer Gynt that Asbjørnsen published in 1848. Ibsen's English translators, William and Charles Archer, derive the name from a root meaning "to bend"; a German translator called it "der Krumme", and in the Russian translation by Anna and Peter Hansen it is Krivaya, "the Crooked One". It has one piece of advice: "Go roundabout, Peer!" Peer shouts "No, through!" and lashes out, but his blows land on nothing: "Forward or back, and it's just as far; out or in, and it's just as strait! He is there! And there! And he's round the bend! No sooner I'm out than I'm back in the ring." The Boyg does not strike back: "The great Boyg conquers, but does not fight."

Critics argued over what it is. Georg Brandes saw in the Boyg the spirit of compromise. The Swedish critic Vasenius saw Peer's inability to take a decisive step — to go through an obstacle instead of skirting round it. For the couple 18-12-21 the second reading fits better. This is a moonlit enemy: shapeless, nocturnal, immune to a quarrel. Such couples rarely break over a big scandal. They spend years going round the same subject — money, parents, an old story, the question of children, a move. Each detour makes sense on its own: "not now", "let's not spoil the evening". Together the detours close into a ring, and inside it the two walk in circles.

In the play the Boyg is not beaten by fists. Church bells and psalm-singing are heard far away, and it "shrinks up to nothing", gasping: "He was too strong. There were women behind him." Before he falls, Peer manages to call to the girl with the psalm-book: "Your clasp-book! Hurl it straight into his eyes!" The fog is lifted not by force but by a voice close by. In a couple that voice belongs to whoever is the first to say out loud what both have been going round.

Remember the ring. Archer's Peer is "back in the ring"; the original is more exact still: as soon as he gets out, he is standing "midt i ringen" — in the very middle of the ring. That ring will come back at the end of the tail.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — The Hanged Man: the half-open door
paragraphs: Act three. Peer is an outlaw living in the forest; he builds a hut and fixes a bar to the door — against "troll-folk, and men, and women", against "cantankerous hobgoblin-thoughts". Solveig comes over the snow on skis. She has left her father, her mother and her little sister, and to those who asked "Whither go you?" she answered, "I go home." "The path I have trodden leads back nevermore." Peer forgets about the bar, yet his words still carry moonlight: "Solveig! Let me look at you! Not too near! Only look at you!" He is ready to carry her in his arms — and to hold her "far out from me", so as not to soil her.

Peer goes to fetch wood, and out of the thicket comes the Woman in Green, the Dovre-King's daughter, with an ugly brat — his son from that night in the mountains. "Even as your hut was builded, mine built itself too," she says, and promises to come every day, sit by them and "ask for my share". Left alone, Peer remembers: "The Boyg said, 'Go roundabout!'—so one must here." Going in to Solveig now would mean to "speak, yet be silent; confess, yet conceal". In the Russian translation this almost turns into a pun: the Boyg is Krivaya, "the Crooked One", and Peer wonders whether to krivit dushoy — literally "to make the soul crooked", the Russian idiom for lying.
Then come five lines on which the whole middle of the tail rests:

— You must wait. It is dark, and I've got something heavy to fetch. — Wait; I will help you; the burden we'll share. — No, stay where you are! I must bear it alone. — …Be my way long or short—you must wait. — Yes, I'll wait!

The stage direction: "Solveig remains standing in the open half-door." On that half-open door the play hangs for decades. In the original Peer's refusal says even more: "Jeg får bære det hele" — "I must carry all of it", literally "the whole". That word, hele, will return in the last scene.

This is the middle of the tail 18-12-21: not betrayal and not a quarrel, but a refused offer to share the burden. Here the Hanged Man has two faces. One carries the weight alone and calls it care: "Don't worry about it, I'll sort it out myself." The other waits and calls it loyalty. Both sacrifices look noble, and together they make a door that is neither open nor shut. Lisovskaya writes that with the Hanged Man a couple takes a long time to commit and often needs a push from outside to marry; in its sacrificial version one partner does everything for the other and nothing for themselves, and the picture outside looks better than the life within. In ordinary life this means years of "after the renovation", "when the project is over", "when things settle down"; an old debt one partner keeps quiet about "so as not to cause worry"; a move that gets discussed every holiday.

But the Hanged Man is not only standing still. It is also the ability to see from the other side, and Lisovskaya notes a rare plus in these couples: the partners sense each other at a distance. Solveig's song is sung thousands of miles from Peer: "Maybe both the winter and spring will pass by, and the next summer too, and the whole of the year; — but thou wilt come one day, that know I full well; and I will await thee, as I promised of old." In her last song she still remembers that very burden: "Is thy burden heavy, take time, take time." In the original Solveig repeats the words of that evening exactly. Peer left saying "jeg har noget tungt at hente" — "I've got something heavy to fetch". She sings: "Har du tungt at hente, så und dig frist" — "if what you went to fetch is heavy, take your time". Wen writes that the Hanged Man raises the question "will the Seeker fall or fly?" and sends the message to "hang in there". The middle of the tail is not a verdict but a pause whose outcome is not written down.

The number of the middle confirms that there is no way round it. The couple's middle is counted from the personal middles: 20 + 19 = 39 → 12. One partner's Sun and the other's Judgement, two cards of light and awakening, fold together into suspension. And if the outer numbers of the tail are added, 18 + 21, the result is the same 39. Whichever way it is counted, the two arrive at the same door.

sections.h2: Main task — The World in the minus: emperor of the earth and the onion
paragraphs: The main task is read through its minus, and Ibsen gives the minus of the World a whole act. In act four Peer is rich, entertains guests on the Moroccan coast and declares his life's goal: "To be Emperor." — "Where?" — "O'er all the world." In the same breath he recalls a Gospel line and retells it his own way: "if you gained the whole wide world, but lost yourself, your gain were but a garland on a cloven skull." And asked what his Self is, he answers: "The world behind my forehead's arch."

Here it is worth going back to the troll hall. The king said that men are taught to be themselves "out yonder, under the shining vault". Peer puts his world behind the arch of his own forehead. In the original both lines use the same word, hvælv, "vault": the world of men lies under the sky, Peer's world under his brow. That is the World in the minus: a whole universe that fits inside one head.

The original holds one more echo, and Archer kept it. The king calls "enough" the "sundering", splitting word — kløvende. And in Peer's version of the Gospel line, the victory of a man who gained the world and lost himself is a garland round a "cloven" temple, kløvet tinding. The troll's "enough" splits, and a world bought without a self crowns a split head.

Then comes the madhouse in Cairo. The director explains that here everyone is "oneself, and nothing whatever besides": "No one has tears for the other's woes; no one has mind for the other's ideas." Peer is crowned with a wreath of straw: "Long life, long life to Self-hood's Kaiser!" And in act five, back in the forest, he peels a wild onion and names every layer: the shipwrecked man, the gold-digger, the Prophet. One layer looks like a crown, and Peer throws it away. There is no kernel: "nothing but swathings — each smaller and smaller."

Lisovskaya describes the World in the minus with scenes that are easy to recognise in these pictures. One partner draws the shared world to their own plan and takes offence if the other has a different map: re-educates, imposes views. Friends and relatives drop away one by one: "we don't need anyone". The relationship goes round the circle of "together — apart", like Peer, who left supposedly for a while and came back decades later. Life becomes a Groundhog Day of roles — parents, hosts, colleagues — and when the roles come off, the middle is empty, like the onion. Waite's divinatory list for the World includes "voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place", and reversed, "inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence". In the play these lists are divided between two people, and neither of them reaches the World alone.

sections.h2: A button on the vest of the world: how the World comes together
paragraphs: In act five an old Peer is visited by the Button-moulder with his casting-ladle: Peer's soul is to be melted down with the rest of the spoilt goods. He is no villain — even the Devil, whom Peer meets a little later, will turn him down — and that is the whole point. "Now, you were designed for a shining button on the vest of the world; but your loop gave way." A button without a loop is only good for melting: there is nothing to sew it to.

Here is the main task of the tail 18-12-21 put in the simplest words. Not an emperor of the world, and not a troll who is "enough" for himself, but a button with a loop: a small place sewn into a larger cloth. Wen writes that the World stands for "oneness with his or her greater calling" and for "the Seeker's importance in the greater cosmic landscape". A couple with this tail builds its world not by walling itself off from everyone, and not when one of the two goes looking for "real life" on the other side of the earth. It builds it when the two acquire a shared loop: a home, a cause, a circle of people they are sewn to together.

The main task is plain addition with no reduction. The partners' personal main tasks, The Chariot (7) and Temperance (14), add up to 21. Our reading: the World is made of movement and measure, and neither the one who only travels nor the one who only waits and keeps can assemble it alone.

Peer understands this before he dares to act. He passes a familiar hut and hears Solveig singing: "One that's remembered,—and one that's forgot. One that has squandered,—and one that has saved.— Oh, earnest!—and never can the game be played o'er! Oh, dread!—here was my Kaiserdom!" In the original it is "O, angst! — Her var mit kejserdom!" Everything he had sought "o'er all the world" stood in the forest, behind a half-open door.

The finale answers the Boyg word for word. Peer walks up to the hut and repeats its words: "Forward and back, and it's just as far. Out and in, and it's just as strait." He stops: "Round about, said the Boyg!" And for the first time in his life: "Ah no; this time at least right through, though the path may be never so strait!" On the threshold stands Solveig, dressed for church, "with a psalm-book wrapped in a kerchief". This is exactly how Peer first saw her at the wedding in act one: the circle of the play closes on the same detail. Solveig gropes for him. Peer sets her a riddle: "Where was I, as myself, as the whole man, the true man? Where was I, with God's sigil upon my brow?" The answer: "In my faith, in my hope, and in my love." In the original Peer asks where he was "den hele, den sande" — the whole one, the true one. That is the word of the World: whole. And it is the same hele he once meant to carry off alone. He turned out to be whole in the place where he had been offered a share of the burden.

But Ibsen does not end on a full stop. Peer hides his face in Solveig's lap — "My mother; my wife; oh, thou innocent woman!" — she sings a lullaby, the sun rises, and from behind the house comes the Button-moulder's voice: "At the last cross-road we will meet again, Peer; and then we'll see whether——; I say no more." There is no verdict, only a reprieve. For a couple this is the most honest moment of the tail. A cradle is a circle too, but in it one holds and the other hides. The main task of the World is a circle in which both are whole: the one who went away comes back by the straight road, and the one who waited stops being a door and becomes a person with a life of their own again.

Peer and Solveig's last meeting falls on Whitsun morning. The church-goers walking through the forest sing of the morning "when the tongues of God's kingdom struck the earth like to flaming steel". After a life lived by the rule "speak, yet be silent", the play ends on the feast of speech. Solveig's name contains the Norwegian sol, "sun", and the last stage direction has her singing "in the full daylight": a tail that began at night ends in broad day.

sections.h2: Clues in Waite: the wolf, the tails and the garland
paragraphs: The pictures of the classic Rider–Waite–Smith deck add three clues to this story. The cards on the site have their own artwork, so what follows is about Waite's cards and his text only.

**The Moon.** On Waite's card a dog and a wolf bay at the moon, and a road runs off between two towers. Waite writes: "The path between the towers is the issue into the unknown. The dog and wolf are the fears of the natural mind in the presence of that place of exit, when there is only reflected light to guide it." At their first meeting Peer called himself a werewolf. The first step of a couple with this tail is taken by reflected light, and the fear in it speaks with an animal's voice.

**The Devil.** The figures chained to the altar on Waite's card have tails. "The figures are tailed, to signify the animal nature," Waite writes, "but there is human intelligence in the faces, and he who is exalted above them is not to be their master for ever." This is Peer in the Dovre-King's hall: the tail tied on, the human eye kept. Waite also recalls Papus's version of the card, where the little demons are replaced by "naked human beings, male and female, who are yoked only to each other", and says "the author may be felicitated on this improved symbolism". For a couple with the Devil at the centre the formula is exact: no one stands above them; their chain is one for two.

**The World.** In Waite this is a female figure dancing inside an oval wreath, "an elliptic garland, as if it were a chain of flowers intended to symbolize all sensible things". Now add up the rings Peer has passed through. The Boyg's ring in the dark, where he stands in the very middle and sees nothing. The onion — rings with nothing at the centre. The straw wreath of "Self-hood's Kaiser". The World card is the same ring, but with a living figure in the middle, and she is dancing. The shape is the same, the content the opposite: the entry of the tail already carries its main task, only in negative.

Ibsen himself supplies the word. The Devil whom Peer meets in act five talks about photography: a picture can be straightforward or negative, and in a negative "the lights and the shades are reversed, and they're apt to seem ugly to commonplace eyes; but for all that the likeness is latent in them, and all you require is to bring it out." The Boyg's ring is the negative of the World's garland. The Hanged Man, who sees everything from the reverse side, is the time it takes the picture to develop. Wen notes "the tau cross in the legs" of the Hanged Man "reemerging in Key 21: The World, suggesting that it is the hanged man who shall attain the fulfillment of the World card, not the mob."

sections.h2: The couple's values: a light in a forest hut
paragraphs: "The couple's values" is the spiritual purpose, the road the two are meant to walk together. For couples with the tail 18-12-21 only two cards appear here: The Hermit in 69.3% and The Moon in 30.7%.

The Hermit in Ibsen is two huts. Before the finale Peer looks back on his life and says to the sun: "Thou beautiful sun, thou hast squandered away thy glory of light in an empty hut. There was no one within it to hearten and warm;— the owner, they tell me, was never at home." A few minutes later he asks the Button-moulder what is shining in the forest, and hears: "Only light from a hut." An empty hut whose owner was never home, and a hut with a light in it. The Hermit among a couple's values is the second: a quiet fire of one's own, a time and place of solitude for each, love shown in deeds rather than speeches. The minus is the same as on Peer's first night in the forest: a bar on the door, each on their own, troubles piling up in silence. When Solveig came, Peer said: "Away, away then with nails and planks! No need now for bars against hobgoblin-thoughts." The value of such a couple is the light in the window, not the bar on the door.

The Moon among the values is the night heath of act five. Thread-balls roll under Peer's feet: "We are thoughts; thou shouldst have thought us." A sighing in the air says "We are songs; thou shouldst have sung us!", and dewdrops fall from the branches: "We are tears unshed for ever. Ice-spears, sharp-wounding, we could have melted." For couples whose values hold the Moon, imagination is not only the entry but also the road: shared dreams, night thoughts, music, everything that lives after dark. This Moon asks one thing: to finish the thoughts, sing the songs, shed the tears — to bring what belongs to the night out into the light.

sections.h2: How the tail 18-12-21 is calculated: an example
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The example is the couple 08.01.1976 and 05.07.1975, calculated by the site's engine.
For 08.01.1976: day 8, month 1, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5. Karmic task 8 + 1 + 5 = 14, centre 8 + 1 + 5 + 14 = 28 → 10. Personal tail: 6-20-14.
For 05.07.1975: day 5, month 7, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Karmic task 5 + 7 + 22 = 34 → 7, centre 5 + 7 + 22 + 7 = 41 → 5. Personal tail: 12-19-7.
The couple's centre is 10 + 5 = 15, The Devil. The couple's values in this example are 9, The Hermit.
A few more facts, checked by running through every date:

ul: The tail 18-12-21 occurs in roughly one couple in 516 (0.194%) and ranks 73rd by frequency among the 97 couple tails.
It is always made the same way: one partner has the personal tail 12-19-7, the other 6-20-14. There are no other combinations.
These couples always have 15 at the centre. A personal matrix never has 15 at the centre: this atmosphere exists only in a couple.

18-12-21 never occurs as a personal karmic tail. In a personal matrix the entry M is the main task D plus the centre. With D = 21, the sum with any centre lies between 24 and 43, and such numbers reduce to 12 at most, so an entry of 18 is impossible.
There are no other couple tails made of 18, 12 and 21: these three cards form a tail only in this order.

sections.h2: What helps a couple with the tail 18-12-21
paragraphs: The cards do not predict how two people's story will end. They show where this couple usually turns off "roundabout". A few habits that follow directly from the plot:

ul: **Name the Boyg.** Find the subject both partners keep going round and say it out loud in a single sentence. Fists cannot beat the Boyg, but a voice makes it dissolve.

**Share the burden.** When one says "I'll handle it myself", ask what exactly is heavy. "Wait; I will help you; the burden we'll share" is the line after which, in Ibsen, everything could have gone differently.

**Wait with a loop.** "You must wait" without an agreement leaves the door half-open. Waiting holds when both know what they are waiting for, what each will do in the meantime and when they will come back to the conversation.
**Check the reflection.** Instead of three night-time versions, ask one daytime question. Moonlight is reflected light: it shows whatever the onlooker brought along.
**Don't scratch the eye.** Accepting small tails for the sake of peace is fine. Seeing what is crooked as beautiful for the sake of calm is not.
**Open the hut.** Friends, family, guests, a shared cause for others. A couple's world should not fit behind one forehead, or even two.

**Travel together.** Lisovskaya advises couples with the World to travel together and to go through difficulties together rather than run from them. Peer crossed half the globe alone; a couple's World is a road both of them walk.

paragraphs: If the waiting or the "burden" comes with fear for one's own safety, reading the tail will not help: that calls for a psychologist, and in danger, the local emergency number.

faq.q: What does 18-12-21 mean in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: It is the karmic tail of a couple's matrix: The Moon at the entry to the task, The Hanged Man in the middle, The World as the main task. The couple comes together over a shared secret, goes through a long pause and learns to build a common whole instead of searching for it separately.

faq.q: Why is the tail 18-12-21 called a programme?
faq.a: Yuliana Lisovskaya, whose book the compatibility calculation follows, calls the triple on a couple's tail a karmic programme. The 18-12-21 programme and the couple's karmic tail 18-12-21 are one and the same thing.

faq.q: Can 18-12-21 appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: Not as a personal karmic tail: in a personal matrix, when the main task is 21, the entry cannot be 18. This triple appears only in the compatibility matrix of two people.

faq.q: Is the tail 18-12-21 a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. The tail shows a couple's task, not its fate: where the two usually get stuck and what they have to learn together. It occurs in roughly one couple in 516, and it contains no forecast.

faq.q: How can a couple quickly tell they have the tail 18-12-21?
faq.a: Look at the partners' personal karmic tails: if one has 12-19-7 and the other 6-20-14, the couple's tail is 18-12-21. There is no other way to get it; the most reliable check is to calculate the couple's matrix from both birth dates.

report: Peer Gynt searched the whole world for his kingdom, and it was waiting for him in a forest hut, behind a half-open door. Ibsen wrote the story in 1867, and the three cards of the tail 18-12-21 appear in it in their own order: The Moon is night and a fairy tale, The Hanged Man is the threshold where two people get stuck, The World is the whole that has to be built by both.

report.h3: A fairy tale that dislikes questions

report: The play opens with his mother's words: "Peer, you're lying!" Peer has just told her how he plunged into the abyss on a reindeer, and how their own reflection rose to meet them from the depths of a mountain tarn. His mother remembers hearing this story as a girl, and it happened to someone else. The first image of the play is a man falling towards his own reflection. Waite calls the light of the Moon a reflection and puts "deception" on its list.

Love begins the same way. At a wedding Peer sees Solveig: "How fair! Did ever you see the like!" She hears his name and pulls her hand away: the gossip about him arrived before he did. He threatens to turn into a troll and come at midnight, and a moment later, "as if in dread", he begs: "Dance with me, lass!" Each meets not a person but an image.

For the couple this is the entry to the task. The two are drawn together by a secret: understanding without words, private pet names, a shared legend about themselves. This is their common language. But the same Moon turns into resistance: **a fairy tale does not like questions.** To "What's wrong?" one answers "Nothing", and by nightfall the other has built three versions and checked none of them. The image made at the start protects the couple as long as nobody touches it — and nobody touches it for years.

report.h3: An enemy that does not fight

report: Then Peer finds himself in pitch darkness, where something slimy and shapeless blocks the way: the Boyg. It has one piece of advice: "Go roundabout, Peer!" Peer punches at nothing: "Forward or back, and it's just as far … No sooner I'm out than I'm back in the ring." And the Boyg replies: "The great Boyg conquers, but does not fight."

Couples with this tail rarely break over a loud scandal. They spend years going round the same subject: money, parents, an old story, a move. Each detour makes sense on its own — "not now", "let's not spoil the evening" — but together the detours close into a ring, and the two walk it in circles. In the play the Boyg is scattered not by fists but by voices from afar. The fog lifts when someone is the first to say out loud what both have been going round.
Solveig comes to Peer's forest hut, leaving her family behind. He goes to fetch wood and runs into his own past. Then come five lines on which the whole middle of the tail rests:

— You must wait. It is dark, and I've got something heavy to fetch. — Wait; I will help you; the burden we'll share. — No, stay where you are! I must bear it alone. — …Be my way long or short—you must wait. — Yes, I'll wait!

The stage direction: "Solveig remains standing in the open half-door." There the play hangs for decades. In the original Peer says "Jeg får bære det hele" — "I must carry all of it", literally "the whole".

This is the Hanged Man of the couple 18-12-21: not betrayal and not a quarrel, but **a refused offer to share the burden.** One carries the weight alone and calls it care: "Don't worry about it, I'll sort it out myself." The other waits and calls it loyalty. Both sacrifices are noble, and together they make a door that is neither open nor shut: years of "after the renovation", "when things settle down".

But the Hanged Man is also a pause whose outcome is not written down. Such partners sense each other at a distance. Decades later Solveig sings to a Peer who is far away, and repeats his words from that evening: if the thing he went to fetch is heavy, let him take his time.

Peer goes off to look for the world. Grown rich, he declares his goal: "To be Emperor." Where? "O'er all the world." He describes his Self like this: "The world behind my forehead's arch." In a madhouse he is crowned with a wreath of straw: "Long life, long life to Self-hood's Kaiser!" In old age he peels an onion, layer after layer, and finds no kernel. This is the World in the minus: a universe that fits inside one head. In a couple's life it is a shared world drawn to one partner's plan, friends dropping away one by one, "we don't need anyone", the circle of "together — apart".

Near the end the Button-moulder comes to Peer and explains why he is to be melted down: "Now, you were designed for a shining button on the vest of the world; but your loop gave way." **The main task of the tail is not a kingdom over the world but a button with a loop:** a small place sewn into a larger cloth — a home, a cause, a circle of people the two are sewn to together.

Passing a familiar hut, Peer hears the song and understands: "Oh, dread!—here was my Kaiserdom!" The Boyg once told him to go roundabout. In the last scene he says: "Ah no; this time at least right through." On the threshold stands Solveig, and Peer sets her a riddle: where was he himself, "the whole man, the true man"? The answer: "In my faith, in my hope, and in my love." In the original he asks where he was "den hele" — whole. The very word with which he once refused to share the burden. **He turned out to be whole in the place where he had been offered a share of it.**

Ibsen does not end on a full stop. Peer hides his face in Solveig's lap, she sings a lullaby, and from behind the house comes: "At the last cross-road we will meet again, Peer; and then we'll see whether——" A cradle is a circle too, but in it one holds and the other hides. A couple's World is a circle in which both are whole: the one who went away comes back by the straight road, and the one who waited becomes a person with a life of their own again, not a door.

What changes the script: naming the subject both keep going round; meeting "I'll handle it myself" with a question about what exactly is heavy; waiting by agreement rather than "be my way long or short"; asking one daytime question instead of building three night-time versions; keeping the door of the hut open to friends and family. If the waiting or the "burden" comes with fear for one's own safety, what is needed is not a reading of the tail but a psychologist, and in danger, a local emergency number or crisis line.
